lessons.title: Ordinal numbers: der erste, der zweite … der einunddreißigste
lessons.goal: Say and read the dates 1 to 31 and use them with am.

grammar.point: An ordinal gives the order: 1 to 19 add -te (odd: erste, dritte, siebte), 20 and up add -ste; after am the ordinal ends in -ten
grammar.oneLine: der dritte Mai. am dritten Mai. 20 and up: -ste.

mistake.why: A date needs the ordinal (fünfte), not the plain number.

terms.meaning: a number that gives the order: first, second, third
the day and the month: the fifth of May
letters at the end of a word

cards.title: Before we start: the order of dates
cards.body: Chapter 6 is about celebrating: dates, birthdays, invitations, plans, a café, and yesterday. Today the first step is the date. To say the third of May you need numbers that give an order: first, second, third.
steps: You already know: am Montag, and the months (chapters 2 and 3)
New today: ordinal numbers, der erste, der dritte, der zwanzigste
By the end you can: say today's date and the date of an event

examples.de: Am ersten Mai habe ich Zeit.
examples.en: On the first of May I have time.
examples.why: New today: the date after am ends in -ten.

examples.en: Today is the eleventh of May.
examples.why: New today: elfte, an ordinal number.

cards.more: Counting says how many. An ordinal says which one in the line, like first or third in a queue. German adds a small ending to the number, mostly -te, and from twenty on -ste. Three are odd: erste, dritte and siebte. That is all. Dates use these numbers every day, so you will say them a lot. The next cards build them in small steps: the odd ones, the ones with -te, the ones with -ste and the dot in 3. Mai.

cards.title: Ordinal numbers: first, second, third
cards.body: Numbers count: eins, zwei, drei. Ordinal numbers give the order: first, second, third. You need them for dates. In German an ordinal has an ending: der erste, der zweite. Here are the first ten. Notice der achte: acht already ends in t, so you add only -e.
cards.more: Think of a race. Numbers say how many runners there are: eins, zwei, drei. Ordinals say who came first, second, third. In German the ordinal is a describing word, so it wears an ending: erste, zweite, dritte. Step 1: find the number. Step 2: add -te. Step 3: watch the odd ones: erste, dritte. Extra example: der vierte Tag = the fourth day.
cards.lead: Your intro said dates need order words. This card gives the first ten of them, first, second, third and so on, so you can start naming days in a month.

deeper.text: German -te is a cousin of English -th: vier-te is four-th. As in English, the first and third are odd: erste and dritte, like first and third. But zweite is regular, because it is just zwei + te. Use the ordinal with der in front when you name a day: der vierte Tag.

cards.title: 11 to 19: add -te
cards.body: From 4 to 19 you add -te to the number. Three words are odd: erste (1), dritte (3) and siebte (7: sieben loses its en). Also learn elfte (11) and zwölfte (12). Then dreizehnte, vierzehnte … are easy.

examples.en: Today is the eleventh of May.
Today is the twelfth of June.
Today is the nineteenth of July.

cards.more: Picture the teens as a ladder. From 13 up they all follow one rule: the number plus -te, so dreizehn becomes dreizehnte and neunzehn becomes neunzehnte. Only the two bottom rungs, elf and zwölf, are special: they add -te to their own letters and give elfte and zwölfte. Step 1: say the number. Step 2: add -te. Step 3: for 11 and 12 look at the table. Extra example: Heute ist der siebzehnte August. = Today is the seventeenth of August.
cards.lead: You know the first ten order words now. This card shows how the teens from eleven to nineteen work, so you can name later days of the month.

deeper.text: Dates stop at 31, so a month needs ordinals from 1 to 31 and no more. That makes the tables small. The words elfte and zwölfte look odd, because they keep the f from elf and zwölf and just add -te. You mostly need to recognise them in dates, not say them fast.

example.en: Today is the seventeenth of July.

cards.title: 20 and up: add -ste
cards.body: From 20 on you add -ste, not -te. zwanzig becomes zwanzigste. For 21 to 31 say the one first, like in the numbers: einundzwanzigste. The biggest day of a month is the 31st: der einunddreißigste.

examples.en: Today is the twentieth of May.
Today is the thirtieth of June.

cards.more: Cut the month into two halves. Days 1 to 19 get -te. Days 20 to 31 get -ste. Step 1: is the number 20 or more? Step 2: add -ste. Step 3: for 21 to 29 say the one first: ein-und-zwanzig-ste. It is the same backwards order you learned for numbers. Extra example: der fünfundzwanzigste Dezember = the 25th of December.
cards.lead: From the teens you move on to twenty and beyond. This card covers the bigger order words, so you can name the last days of a month, up to the 31st.

deeper.text: Why -ste after 20? Every number that ends in -zig takes -ste: zwanzig-ste, dreißig-ste. You will meet the same ending later for big numbers, like hundertste. In 21 to 31 only the last piece changes, and the one stays first: ein-und-zwanzig-ste. So the rule of thumb is simple: up to 19 add -te, from 20 add -ste.

example.en: Today is the twenty-fifth of July.

cards.title: Read the dot: 3. Mai = der dritte Mai
cards.body: When you write a date with digits, a dot after the number shows an ordinal. 3. Mai is read der dritte Mai. 20. Mai is der zwanzigste Mai. No dot means a plain number.

examples.en: Today is the third of May.
Today is the twelfth of June.

cards.more: The little dot is a secret sign. It says: read this number as a first, second, third. So 3. Mai is not drei Mai. It is der dritte Mai. Picture a sticker on the number: the dot sticker means ordinal. Step 1: see the number with a dot. Step 2: turn it into the ordinal. Step 3: add the month. Extra example: 8. August = der achte August.
cards.lead: Dates are often written with digits and a dot. This card shows what that dot means and how to read it aloud, so you can say the date when you see 3. Mai.

deeper.text: In a written date the dot is a silent ending: it stands for -te or -ste. So 24. Dezember is read der vierundzwanzigste Dezember. You will see this in every Kalender (calendar), on tickets and in emails. 24.12. means the 24th of December: day first, then month. This is the opposite of the US order.

cards.title: After am: -te becomes -ten
cards.body: To say on the third of May, you say am dritten Mai. The date ends in -ten after am. Learn am + …-ten as one piece. Why the n? That comes in a later chapter. For now: copy the pattern.

examples.en: On the first of May I have time.

examples.de: Am dritten Juni fahre ich nach Wien.
examples.en: On the third of June I go to Vienna.

examples.de: Am zwanzigsten August spiele ich Tennis.
examples.en: On the twentieth of August I play tennis.

cards.more: You already know am Montag. Now the date works the same way: am + date. The only new thing is the ending. After am, the date word ends in -n: ersten, dritten, zehnten, zwanzigsten. Do not ask why yet. Step 1: write am. Step 2: take the ordinal. Step 3: put -n on the end. Extra example: am siebten Mai = on the seventh of May.
cards.lead: Now you can name a date in its order form. This card shows the form you need after am, so you can say on which day something happens.

deeper.text: After am the ordinal always ends in -n, and every date works the same. So there is only one new thing to learn: am + the ordinal + -n. English only adds on (the third, on the third), but German also changes the ending. Copy the pattern for now.

example.en: On the twelfth of June I learn German.

cards.title: A whole date in a sentence
cards.body: You can say the date in two ways. Heute ist der fünfte Mai tells a fact. Am fünften Mai … says on that day. When the date starts the sentence, the verb is still part 2, as always.

cards.more: Remember the verb chair from chapter 1: the verb always sits in part 2. The date can fill part 1. Then the verb sits in part 2, and ich moves behind it. Step 1: Am fünften Mai (part 1). Step 2: habe (part 2). Step 3: ich. Step 4: Zeit. Extra example: Am zweiten Mai arbeite ich. = On the second of May I work.
cards.lead: Dates can sit inside whole sentences now. This card gives two ways to use them, a plain fact and a sentence about a day, so you can say what you do on a date.

deeper.text: Which date is today? Ask Welches Datum ist heute? and answer Heute ist der … with the ordinal. Welches Datum means which date. Use Heute ist der … for a fact and Am … when you say on which day something happens. They look similar, so choose by the job. Natives also ask Der Wievielte ist heute? and the answer is the same: Heute ist der …

lessons.title: Birthdays and dates: Wann hast du Geburtstag?
lessons.goal: Ask and tell when your birthday is, wish someone well and read a 24-hour time.

grammar.point: You have a birthday: Ich habe am ersten Mai Geburtstag; wann asks for the date; after 12 o'clock the 24-hour clock keeps counting, so take away 12 (18 Uhr = 6 pm)
grammar.oneLine: Wann hast du Geburtstag? – Am ersten Mai. Die Party ist um 18 Uhr.

mistake.wrong: Ich bin am ersten Mai Geburtstag.
mistake.right: Ich habe am ersten Mai Geburtstag.
mistake.why: In German you have a birthday (haben), you are not one.

terms.meaning: the thing a verb acts on: Geschenk in Mira kauft ein Geschenk
a group of words you learn as one piece
a clock that counts to 24: 18 Uhr is 6 pm

cards.title: Before we start: birthdays
cards.body: A friend asks: "When is your birthday?" You want to answer and to invite people to the party. Today you use the date to talk about birthdays. German has a special way to say it.
steps: You already know: haben, for example Ich habe Hunger (chapter 2)
New today: Ich habe Geburtstag, and the date with am
By the end you can: say when your birthday is and wish someone a happy birthday

examples.de: Ich habe am ersten Mai Geburtstag.
examples.en: My birthday is on the first of May.
examples.why: New today: German says I have a birthday, with the date in the middle.
New today: Wann hast du Geburtstag?

cards.more: In English a birthday is something that is. In German it is something that you have, just like hunger or time. So the sentence is one you already know: ich habe plus a noun. Then you slide the date into the middle with am, and the verb keeps its chair 2. You will also learn two nice chunks for wishing someone well, and how to read a clock time on an invitation. Step by step in the next cards.

cards.title: Wann hast du Geburtstag?
cards.body: In German you do not say my birthday is. You say you have a birthday: Ich habe Geburtstag. The date goes in the middle with am: Ich habe am ersten Mai Geburtstag. Geburtstag is the object of haben.

examples.de: Ich habe am dritten Juni Geburtstag.
examples.en: My birthday is on the third of June.

examples.de: Mira hat am siebten Mai Geburtstag.
examples.en: Mira's birthday is on the seventh of May.

cards.more: Imagine a birthday is something you own, like a hat. You do not say I am a birthday. You say I have a birthday. So we use haben, which you know: ich habe, du hast, er hat. Step 1: Ich habe. Step 2: am + the date. Step 3: Geburtstag. Extra example: Ben hat am zehnten Juli Geburtstag. = Ben has his birthday on the tenth of July.
cards.lead: You can say dates now, so the next question people ask at parties is when a birthday is. This card shows how to ask it and how to answer with a date.

deeper.text: Geburtstag is Geburt (birth) + Tag (day): a birth-day. Ich habe Geburtstag can mean that it is my birthday today, so you can ask Hast du heute Geburtstag? On a form you will see a different word, das Geburtsdatum, the date you were born. So Geburtstag is the party day, and Geburtsdatum is the fact on your passport.

cards.title: Answer, and say my and your
cards.body: A short answer is just the date: Am zwanzigsten Mai. You can also use Wann ist dein Geburtstag? Mein Geburtstag ist am …. Here dein means your and mein means my. You know these from chapter 5.

examples.de: Mein Geburtstag ist am achten Juli.
examples.en: My birthday is on the eighth of July.

rows: Ich habe am ersten Mai Geburtstag.
Mein Geburtstag ist am ersten Mai.

cards.more: Two ways to ask, same meaning. Way 1: Wann hast du Geburtstag? Way 2: Wann ist dein Geburtstag? dein is the your that goes with a friend (du). mein is the my that goes with ich. Step 1: pick your question. Step 2: answer with am + date. Extra example: Mein Geburtstag ist am ersten Mai. = My birthday is on the first of May.
cards.lead: You know how to say your birthday. This card gives a short answer, and the question with dein, so you can ask a friend when theirs is.

deeper.text: Short answers sound natural: Wann hast du Geburtstag? Am ersten Mai. You do not need the whole sentence. The answer starts with am, not um, because a date is a day, and days take am. Germans rarely add the year when they talk about a birthday. Then ask back: Und du? That keeps the talk going.

cards.title: Congratulations: learn two chunks
cards.body: Two chunks for a birthday: Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag! and Alles Gute! Learn each as one piece. You will see why it is zum in a later chapter. Answer with Danke!
cards.more: A chunk is a little Lego block. You do not take it apart. You just snap it on. Herzlichen Glückwunsch zum Geburtstag! is one block. Say it to a friend on the day. Alles Gute! is a shorter block for any good wish. Step 1: smile. Step 2: say the whole block. Step 3: say Danke when you get it. Extra example: Herzlichen Glückwunsch, Leon! = Congratulations, Leon!
cards.lead: Birthdays come with good wishes. This card gives two fixed phrases for saying happy birthday and a short reply, so you can congratulate a friend right away.

deeper.text: Friends say Alles Gute zum Geburtstag! on the day itself. It is considered bad luck to congratulate early, so Germans wait. A friend who forgets and says it a day too soon may even get a funny look. Mira and Ben will not forget it. Say it on the day, and say the name after a comma.

cards.title: Clock times on invitations: 24 hours
cards.body: You know um … Uhr (at … o'clock) from chapter 5. On invitations people often use the 24-hour clock. After noon the clock keeps counting, so take away 12: 18 Uhr is 6 in the evening. The word um comes before the time.
cards.more: Think of the clock going round twice a day. After 12 it keeps counting: 13, 14, 15 … So 15 Uhr is 3 in the afternoon. Step 1: see a number over 12. Step 2: take away 12. Step 3: that is the normal time. 19 Uhr is 7 in the evening. Extra example: Die Party ist um 19 Uhr. = The party is at 7 pm.
cards.lead: Invitations often use the long clock. This card matches those times to the ones you already know, so you can read the time of a party on a card.

deeper.text: On invitations and tickets people write 18:30 Uhr, but at the party they say halb sieben (half way to seven). So the same time has a written form and a spoken form. Both are normal. Practise reading the written one and saying the spoken one.

cards.title: feiern: to celebrate
cards.body: feiern is a regular verb: take off -en and add the ending. ich feiere, du feierst, er/sie feiert, wir feiern, ihr feiert, sie feiern. You know this pattern from chapter 1 and 2.
cards.more: feiern is like kochen or spielen: nothing odd. Think of a template: stem plus ending. Step 1: take off -en, and feier is left. Step 2: add the ending for the person: ich feiere, du feierst, er feiert, wir feiern, ihr feiert, sie feiern. Notice that er and ihr look the same, and wir and sie look like the infinitive. Extra example: Mira feiert am Sonntag. = Mira celebrates on Sunday.
cards.lead: Now you can say when a birthday is and invite people. This card gives the verb for celebrating, so you can say what you do on a day with friends.

deeper.text: feiern can take an object: you celebrate something. Ich feiere meinen Geburtstag. As always, the masculine object changes: mein becomes meinen, but a feminine word like Party stays the same. Notice that wir and sie feiern look just like the infinitive.

cards.title: Plan a party: verb and object
cards.body: For a party you buy things. kaufen takes an object. You know the accusative from chapter 4: only masculine changes. Ich kaufe einen Kuchen. Ich kaufe ein Geschenk. Ich kaufe eine Torte.
cards.more: Quick memory check from chapter 4. Only the blue masculine box changes: der becomes den, ein becomes einen. The red and green boxes stay the same. A Kuchen is masculine, so einen Kuchen. A Torte is feminine, so eine Torte. A Geschenk is neuter, so ein Geschenk. Step 1: find the gender. Step 2: is it masculine? Then einen. Extra example: Ich kaufe einen Saft. = I buy a juice.
cards.lead: A party needs food and presents. This card shows the verb for buying and the small change in the endings that comes with it, so you can say what you buy for a party.

deeper.text: You can also say what you do not buy with kein. The endings are the same as for ein: keinen Kuchen, keine Torte, kein Geschenk. For a name like Anna or Leon, nothing changes. A party list is a good place to practise the accusative with food and presents.

example.en: Herr Ali does not buy a present.

lessons.title: Invitations: read, write, say yes or no
lessons.goal: Read and write a short invitation, answer it, and find the key facts in a text or a radio tip.

grammar.point: An invitation asks a yes/no question (Kommst du?); with möchten and kann the second verb goes to the end; leider starts a polite no
grammar.oneLine: Möchtest du kommen? Leider kann ich nicht kommen.

mistake.why: After Leider the verb is still part 2: kann. The infinitive kommen goes to the end.

terms.meaning: a letter or message that asks someone to come
the basic form of a verb: kommen, spielen
the main facts in a text: who, what, when, where

cards.title: Before we start: invitations
cards.body: Mira invites you to a party. You read it, decide, and answer: yes or no. Today you learn to read and write a short invitation and to answer it politely.
steps: You already know: Möchtest du einen Kaffee? with the verb first (chapter 4)
New today: Möchtest du kommen? and polite answers like Ja, gern and Leider …
By the end you can: read an invitation for the key facts and say yes or no

examples.why: New today: the second verb goes to the end, like in the bracket.
New today: a polite no with leider and kann.

cards.more: An invitation is like a small letter with four boxes: a greeting, the news, the plan and a question. When you read one, you do not need every word. You just hunt for the key facts: who, what, when and where. When you answer, you use what you know, a yes/no question with the verb first, and the bracket with kann at the end. The next cards show you how to say yes, how to say no nicely and how to read like a detective.

cards.title: An invitation: four parts
cards.body: A friendly invitation (die Einladung) has four parts. A greeting (Liebe Mira,), the news (Ich habe am Samstag Geburtstag.), the plan (Die Party ist um 18 Uhr.) and a question (Kommst du?). Then you end with Viele Grüße and your name.

examples.en: I have my birthday on Saturday.

cards.more: Think of a letter as four little boxes. Box 1: hello. Box 2: why you write. Box 3: when and where. Box 4: a question, so your friend can answer. Step 1: pick the greeting: Liebe for a woman, Lieber for a man. Step 2: write your news. Step 3: ask. Step 4: say bye with Viele Grüße. You can write it on a card (die Karte) or in a message. Extra example: Lieber Ben, hast du am Samstag Zeit? = Dear Ben, do you have time on Saturday?
cards.lead: You have read about parties. Now you write one. This card names each part of a short invitation to a friend, so you know what to put in your own message.

deeper.text: Lieb means dear. Add -er for a man and -e for a woman: Lieber Ben, Liebe Mira. After the greeting comma the next line starts with a small letter, even though it is a new line: Liebe Mira, then ich habe am Samstag Geburtstag. Only nouns and names keep a capital letter. The closing Viele Grüße has no comma.

cards.title: Ask someone to come
cards.body: To invite someone, ask a yes/no question: the verb goes first. Kommst du? is short. Möchtest du kommen? is polite. With möchten (chapter 4) the second verb goes to the end: kommen. Hast du am Samstag Zeit? also works.

examples.en: Would you like to come on Saturday?
Do you have time on Saturday?

cards.more: Three easy ways to invite, all yes/no questions. The verb jumps to the front, like in chapter 2. With möchtest there are two verbs. The first verb stays near the front. The second verb is the infinitive and rides to the very end, like the last wagon of a train. Step 1: Möchtest du … Step 2: the other words. Step 3: kommen last. Extra example: Möchtest du am Sonntag kommen? = Would you like to come on Sunday?
cards.lead: You can write the news and the plan. Now you need a question to invite someone. This card shows friendly ways to ask a yes or no question, so you can ask a friend to come.

deeper.text: The difference is only the verb. Kommst du? is short and warm. Möchtest du kommen? is polite. With someone you do not know well, use Sie: Möchten Sie kommen? Sie takes möchten, and the other verb stays at the end.

example.en: Would you like to come on Saturday?

cards.title: Say yes
cards.body: To say yes, keep it warm and short. Ja, gern! Ja, ich komme gern. Super, ich komme! You know gern from chapter 2. Add a thank you: Vielen Dank! (Thank you very much.) Learn Vielen Dank as one chunk.
cards.more: A yes should sound happy. Ja, gern! is the quickest. If you want a full sentence, use ich komme and add gern at the end. gern means with pleasure. Step 1: say Ja. Step 2: say ich komme. Step 3: add gern. Step 4: say Vielen Dank. Extra example: Ja, ich komme gern. Vielen Dank! = Yes, I will gladly come. Thank you very much!
cards.lead: Someone has invited you, so you need to answer. This card gives warm and short words for saying yes, so you can accept with a friendly tone.

deeper.text: gern is a small word with a big job. Add it to any verb to say that you like to do it: Ich komme gern. It usually stands after the verb. By itself, Gern! means gladly or with pleasure. If you add sehr, it gets stronger: sehr gern.

cards.title: Say no politely: leider, schade, kann
cards.body: To say no, begin with Leider (unfortunately). Leider habe ich keine Zeit. Or use kann (from können, to be able to) from chapter 5: Leider kann ich nicht kommen. The second verb goes to the end. Your friend may answer Schade! (what a pity).

examples.why: Leider is part 1; habe is part 2.

examples.de: Ich kann am Samstag nicht kommen.
examples.why: nicht comes before the last verb.

cards.more: Saying no is easy if you copy this pattern. Part 1: Leider. Part 2: kann, the verb. Then ich and nicht. Last of all comes kommen, the infinitive. It is the train again: the first verb is the engine, the infinitive is the last wagon. can in German: ich kann, du kannst, er kann. Extra example: Leider kann ich am Sonntag nicht kommen. = Unfortunately I cannot come on Sunday.
cards.lead: Saying yes is easy, but saying no needs care. This card gives polite ways to refuse, with a word for unfortunately and a reason, so you do not sound rude.

deeper.text: Leider (unfortunately) softens a no. The reason can follow in a second short sentence: Leider kann ich nicht kommen. Ich habe keine Zeit. The reason does not have to be long. A short, honest no is fine in German. Put leider first, then the verb in part 2.

example.de: Leider habe ich am Samstag keine Zeit.
example.en: Unfortunately I have no time on Saturday.

cards.title: Read for key facts: who, what, when, where
cards.body: You do not need every word. Look for four key facts: who, what, when and where. Look for names, then am and um for the time, and in for the place. Ignore words you do not know.

examples.en: Anna has her birthday on Saturday.
examples.why: Who? Anna. What? Birthday. When? am Samstag.

cards.more: Imagine you are a detective with four questions. Who? Look for a name. What? Look for a noun like Party or Konzert. When? Look for am or um. Where? Look for in. You do not have to understand the rest. Step 1: find the four clues. Step 2: write them down. Step 3: done. Extra example: Das Konzert ist am Freitag um 20 Uhr in Wien. = Who? none. What? concert. When? Friday 8 pm. Where? Vienna.
cards.lead: Invitations and texts have many words you may not know. This card teaches you to find four key facts, so you can understand the most important part even when you miss words.

deeper.text: You do not need to decode every word. Hunt for the four facts like a detective. German helps you: all nouns have a capital letter, so names and places stand out on the page. Numbers like 18 Uhr also jump out. Read the capital letters first.

example.de: Das Fest ist am Samstag in Hamburg.
example.en: The party is on Saturday in Hamburg.

cards.title: A radio tip
cards.body: A radio tip gives you the key facts in one or two sentences. Listen for the four facts. Radiotipp: Das Konzert ist am Freitag um 20 Uhr in Hamburg. You can understand it without knowing every word.

examples.de: Das Konzert ist am Freitag um 20 Uhr.
examples.en: The concert is on Friday at 8 pm.
examples.why: What? Konzert. When? am Freitag, um 20 Uhr.

examples.de: Der Film ist am Samstag um 19 Uhr.
examples.en: The film is on Saturday at 7 pm.
examples.why: What? Film. When? am Samstag, um 19 Uhr.

examples.de: Das Fest ist am Sonntag in Wien.
examples.en: The party is on Sunday in Vienna.
examples.why: What? Fest. When? am Sonntag. Where? in Wien.

cards.more: A radio voice is fast. You cannot catch every word, and that is fine. Catch only the four key facts. First the thing: Konzert, Film, Fest. Then the day: am Freitag. Then the time: um 20 Uhr. Then the place: in Hamburg. Step 1: listen once for the thing. Step 2: listen again for the day and time. Extra example: Das Fest ist am Samstag um 15 Uhr in Wien. = The party is on Saturday at 3 pm in Vienna.
cards.lead: Now you use the four facts on a short radio tip. This card shows how to catch them when you listen, so you can understand an event announcement without reading it.

deeper.text: A radio tip has no pictures, so the words do the work. They often come in the same order: when, then where. Listen for the day and the time (am Freitag um 20 Uhr) and then for the place (in Wien). Learn to hear this order as a pattern.

example.de: Das Konzert ist am Sonntag um 19 Uhr in Wien.
example.en: The concert is on Sunday at 7 pm in Vienna.

lessons.title: Separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end
lessons.goal: Use anrufen, einkaufen, aufstehen, mitkommen and anfangen in sentences and questions.

grammar.point: A separable verb splits: the main verb goes to part 2, the prefix goes to the very end
grammar.oneLine: Ich rufe Mira an. Wann stehst du auf? Kommst du mit?

mistake.why: The prefix an leaves the verb and goes to the end of the sentence.

terms.meaning: a verb with a prefix that breaks off and goes to the end of the sentence
a small word at the front of a verb: an, auf, ein, mit
the last verb part in a sentence

cards.title: Before we start: verbs in two pieces
cards.body: Do you call your friend? Do you come along? Some German verbs split in two when you use them. Today you meet the first of them. The sentence rule you know stays the same, but a little piece moves to the end.
steps: You already know: the verb is part 2 and the object comes after it (Ich treffe Mira)
New today: separable verbs, where a small prefix jumps to the end
By the end you can: say Ich rufe Mira an and ask Wann stehst du auf?

examples.why: New today: anrufen splits, rufe is part 2 and an goes to the end.
New today: the prefix goes last in a question, too.

cards.more: Think of a train with a small last carriage. Most verbs are one whole train. A separable verb is a train with a detachable last carriage: the engine is rufen, the carriage is an. In the sentence the engine stays in chair 2 and the carriage rolls all the way to the end. You have seen this shape before, the bracket from chapter 5. In the next cards you will learn five of these verbs and how they work in questions.

cards.title: A verb in two pieces
cards.body: Some German verbs have a small prefix at the front: an-rufen (to call). In a sentence they break into two pieces. The main verb goes to part 2. The prefix jumps to the very end. The prefix has the colour of the second verb.

examples.why: rufe is part 2; an goes last.
ruft is part 2; an goes last.
rufen is part 2; an goes last.

cards.more: Imagine a train with two wagons that can be unhooked. The infinitive anrufen is the whole train. In a sentence you unhook it. The front wagon, rufen, goes to the verb chair in part 2. The little wagon, an, rides all the way to the end of the sentence. They belong together, even when far apart. Step 1: split an | rufen. Step 2: verb in part 2. Step 3: an at the end. Extra example: Anna ruft Mira an. = Anna calls Mira.
cards.lead: Now you can make plans with friends. This card shows a kind of verb that splits into two parts in a sentence, so you can say you call a friend.

deeper.text: The prefix is a small word that changes the meaning. rufen means to shout or call out, anrufen means to telephone (das Telefon is the phone). English does the same with phrasal verbs: call up, get up, come along. If you know call up, you know anrufen. The idea is old and simple.

cards.title: Five separable verbs
cards.body: Learn these five. They are called separable verbs because they separate. anrufen (to call), einkaufen (to shop), aufstehen (to get up), mitkommen (to come along), anfangen (to begin). Each prefix goes to the end.
cards.more: Five verbs, five little prefixes. an, ein, auf, mit, an. Look at how the word is built: the prefix is on the front, and the verb you know is behind it: kaufen, stehen, kommen, rufen. In the sentence you keep the verb you know in part 2. The prefix goes last. Step 1: find the prefix. Step 2: use the old verb. Step 3: prefix last. Extra example: Ich komme mit. = I come along.
cards.lead: You learned how one verb splits. This card gives five more verbs of the same kind, for calling, shopping, getting up, coming along and starting, so you can talk about your day.

deeper.text: English has the same split: get up, come along. In German the infinitive is written as one word: aufstehen. Only in the sentence does it split. So when you learn a verb, always learn it with its prefix: say aufstehen, never just stehen. The two can mean very different things.

cards.title: Questions: the prefix still goes last
cards.body: In a yes/no question the verb is first. In a W-question the verb is in part 2. In both cases the prefix goes to the very end. Kommst du mit? Wann stehst du auf?
cards.more: A question just moves the verb. The prefix never moves: it always waits at the end. Yes/no question: the verb goes first, like in chapter 2. W-question: the question word is part 1, the verb is part 2, like in chapter 1. Then the prefix sits at the end. Step 1: choose the question type. Step 2: put the verb where it goes. Step 3: prefix last. Extra example: Wann kaufst du ein? = When do you shop?
cards.lead: You can now make statements with split verbs. This card shows where the split part goes in a yes or no question and in a W-question, so you can ask someone if they are coming along.

deeper.text: In a question the prefix still waits at the end. Kommst du mit? So the last thing you hear is the prefix, and it can change the whole meaning. That is why you must listen to the very end. A short answer is easy: Ja, gern! or Ja, ich komme mit.

cards.title: aufstehen: all the forms
cards.body: The main part of the verb follows the normal endings. Take off -en from stehen: steh + ending. ich stehe, du stehst, er/sie steht, wir stehen, ihr steht, sie/Sie stehen. The prefix auf waits at the end.
cards.more: You already know all these endings from chapters 1 and 2. Only the prefix is new. Step 1: take stehen. Step 2: give it its ending for the person: ich stehe, du stehst. Step 3: put auf at the end. Same for every separable verb. aufstehen, anrufen, einkaufen, mitkommen all work like this. Extra example: Wir kaufen ein. = We shop.
cards.lead: The verb for getting up can change for each person. This card gives the full set of its forms, so you can say when you and other people get up.

deeper.text: The ending belongs to the main verb only. The prefix never takes an ending: auf stays auf for every person. So you conjugate stehen as usual and add auf at the end. It helps to think of the prefix as a small tag that never changes.

example.de: Wir stehen am Samstag spät auf.
example.en: We get up late on Saturday.

cards.title: Time first: the verb is still part 2
cards.body: You can start the sentence with a time word. The verb is still part 2. The prefix still goes to the end. Um 7 Uhr stehe ich auf. Am Samstag kaufen wir ein.

examples.why: Object in the middle: prefix still last.

cards.more: Think of a sentence as a train with 4 seats: seat 1, seat 2, then the rest, then the end. Part 1 can be anything: ich, a time, a day. Part 2 is always the verb. The prefix always takes the last seat. Step 1: choose part 1. Step 2: the verb. Step 3: the subject, if it is not in part 1. Step 4: the other words. Step 5: the prefix. Extra example: Morgens stehe ich früh auf. = In the morning I get up early.
cards.lead: You can start a sentence with a time or a thing and still keep the verbs in order. This card shows how, so you can say when you get up or go shopping.

deeper.text: Start with the time when it is the news. Then comes the verb, then the subject, and the prefix is the last word, like a full stop. In long sentences, listen for the end. Remember früh, which means early, like in früh aufstehen, to get up early.

example.de: Am Montag stehe ich früh auf.
example.en: On Monday I get up early.

cards.title: anfangen and ankommen
cards.body: anfangen (to begin) works like fahren: for er/sie the a becomes ä: er fängt … an. ankommen (to arrive) is regular: er kommt … an. A time or a thing can begin or arrive: Der Film fängt um 20 Uhr an. Der Zug kommt um 8 Uhr an.

examples.de: Der Film fängt um 20 Uhr an.
Der Zug kommt um 8 Uhr an.
Der Kurs fängt am Montag an.
examples.why: der Kurs = the course; anfangen: fängt … an.

cards.more: You know fahren: ich fahre, du fährst, er fährt. The a jumps to ä for du and er/sie. anfangen does the same. ich fange … an, du fängst … an, er fängt … an. ankommen has no change: ich komme … an, du kommst … an. Step 1: say the verb for the person. Step 2: a to ä for du and er/sie in anfangen. Step 3: prefix last. Extra example: Das Konzert fängt um 20 Uhr an. = The concert starts at 8 pm.
cards.lead: Some split verbs change their vowel for du and er. This card shows two common ones, for starting and arriving, so you can say when a film begins or a train comes in.

deeper.text: Do not mix up anfangen (to begin) and ankommen (to arrive). They both have an, but the main verbs are different: fangen and kommen. Wann kommst du an? is the standard question about arrival. It means When are you arriving? Listen for the verb to know which one it is.

lessons.title: Separable verbs with modals, and asking someone to join
lessons.goal: Say that you must, can or want to do something with a separable verb, and invite a friend to join you.

grammar.point: With a modal verb, the separable verb stays in one piece at the end; invite with Möchtest du ins Kino gehen? Kommst du mit?
grammar.oneLine: Ich muss um 7 Uhr aufstehen. Kannst du mitkommen?

mistake.wrong: Ich muss um 7 Uhr auf stehen.
mistake.why: With a modal verb the separable verb does not split: it goes to the end as one word.

terms.meaning: a helper verb: müssen, können, wollen, möchten
the basic form of a verb; it goes to the end after a modal
a group of words you learn as one piece: ins Kino

cards.title: Before we start: separable verbs with can and must
cards.body: I must get up at seven. Can you come along? Last lesson the prefix jumped to the end. Now two things from this chapter and the last meet: the modal bracket and the separable verb.
steps: You already know: a modal in part 2 and the second verb at the end (chapter 5), and the prefix at the end
New today: with a modal, the separable verb stays together as one word at the end
By the end you can: say Ich muss um 7 Uhr aufstehen and ask Kannst du mitkommen?

examples.en: I must get up at seven.
examples.why: New today: with muss, aufstehen is one word at the end.

cards.more: Remember the train with the detachable carriage? When a helper verb takes the first handle of the parcel, the train does not need to split. The helper verb sits in chair 2, and the whole train aufstehen, engine and carriage together, rides in the last place. So there is no new rule. You just combine two things you know. The next cards go over the modal bracket again, then how to invite someone to join you.

cards.title: Modal verbs: a quick refresher
cards.body: You know modal verbs from chapter 5: müssen (must), können (can), wollen (want to) and möchten (would like to). The modal is in part 2. The other verb is an infinitive and goes to the very end.
cards.more: A modal verb is a helper. It says how you do something: must, can, want. The helper takes the verb chair in part 2. The real action verb turns into an infinitive and rides to the end, like the last wagon. Step 1: choose the helper and give it its ending. Step 2: put your other words in the middle. Step 3: infinitive last. Extra example: Ich möchte schwimmen. = I would like to swim.
cards.lead: The intro put two chapter ideas together. This card reminds you of the modal verbs you already know, so you can build the same sentence shape with them again.

deeper.text: möchten is a little odd in the table. ich möchte and er möchte end in -e, while müssen, können and wollen have no ending there. It is only a small difference, but it is easy to notice. For all four, the other verb goes to the end.

example.en: She would like to go home.

cards.title: A separable verb with a modal stays together
cards.body: With a modal verb, the separable verb does not split. It goes to the end as one word: the infinitive. Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf. But: Ich muss um 7 Uhr aufstehen. Only the modal takes an ending.

examples.en: I must get up at 7 o'clock.
examples.why: Modal part 2; aufstehen together at the end.

examples.en: We want to shop on Saturday.
examples.why: Modal part 2; einkaufen together at the end.
Modal first; mitkommen together at the end.

cards.more: Here the two wagons stay hooked together. With a modal, the separable verb is an infinitive, and an infinitive never splits. It is like a sealed box at the end of the sentence. Compare: Ich stehe auf (split, no modal). Ich muss aufstehen (together, with modal). Step 1: is there a modal? Step 2: yes? Keep the verb in one piece. Step 3: put it last. Extra example: Ich möchte anrufen. = I would like to call.
cards.lead: A modal verb changes how the split verb behaves. This card shows what the verb looks like at the end of the sentence, so you can say you must get up early.

deeper.text: The separable verb is back to its dictionary form at the end of the sentence: aufstehen, einkaufen. So the sentence with a modal is easier than the one without: nothing splits, and the infinitive is just the word you would look up. Only the modal has an ending.

example.en: Ben has to go shopping today.

cards.title: Where to? ins Kino, in den Park
cards.body: To say where you go, learn these chunks: ins Kino, ins Café, in den Park, in die Stadt. They are whole pieces. You will see why they look like this in chapter 7. Use them with gehen: Ich gehe ins Kino.
cards.more: Do not take these apart. Learn them like names of places. ins Kino. ins Café. in den Park. in die Stadt. They answer the question Wohin? = where to? Step 1: ask Wohin gehst du? Step 2: pick a chunk. Step 3: put gehen in part 2. Extra example: Wohin gehst du? Ich gehe ins Café. = Where are you going? I am going to the café.
cards.lead: You can say when and what you do. Now you need to say where you go. This card gives short chunks for common places like the cinema, the café and the park, so you can say where you are heading.

deeper.text: In your Freizeit (free time) you often say where you go. With gehen you can add a time before the place: Ich gehe um acht Uhr ins Kino. The time comes first and the place second. The question for the place is Wohin gehst du? The answer is often one of the chunks: ins Kino, ins Café.

example.de: Wir gehen am Samstag ins Café.
example.en: On Saturday we go to the café.

cards.title: Invite someone to join you
cards.body: A good invitation has three steps. 1. Ask if the person has time: Hast du am Samstag Zeit? 2. Say your plan: Möchtest du ins Kino gehen? 3. Ask: Kommst du mit? You can also ask Hast du Lust? (Do you feel like it?)

examples.en: Do you have time on Saturday?
Would you like to go to the cinema?

examples.de: Das ist eine Idee! Wir gehen zusammen ins Kino.
examples.en: That is an idea! We go to the cinema together.
examples.why: die Idee = the idea; zusammen = together.

cards.more: Three little steps, like knocking, opening and walking in. Step 1: Hast du Zeit? You check if the door is open. Step 2: your plan: Möchtest du ins Kino gehen? Step 3: Kommst du mit? Now the person can say yes or no. The question Hast du Lust? is a friendly short version. Extra example: Hast du Lust? Wir gehen in den Park. = Do you feel like it? We are going to the park.
cards.lead: You now have all the parts for making plans. This card gives three steps for inviting a friend, so you can ask about their time, name a plan and ask them to join you.

deeper.text: Hast du Lust? is literally Do you have desire? That sounds strong in English, but Lust just means feel like it. It is friendly and relaxed. With a thing, add auf: Hast du Lust auf Pizza? auf means for or on here. Learn the whole chunk Lust auf.

cards.title: Agree a time and a place
cards.body: Ask for the time with Wann …? or Um wie viel Uhr …? Learn Um wie viel Uhr as a chunk: At what time? Then name the place with a short sentence. Wann fängt der Film an? Um 20 Uhr. The prefix of anfangen goes last.

examples.de: Um wie viel Uhr fängt das Konzert an?
examples.en: At what time does the concert begin?

rows: Um wie viel Uhr fängt das Konzert an?

cards.more: To meet a friend you need two facts: time and place. Ask Wann? or Um wie viel Uhr? for the time. Remember anfangen: the prefix an waits at the end. For the place, use the little words you know: hier, da, dort. Step 1: ask for the time. Step 2: ask for the place. Step 3: repeat both to be safe. Extra example: Der Film fängt um 20 Uhr an. = The film starts at 8 pm.
cards.lead: A plan needs a time. This card shows how to ask when something starts and what time you agree on, so you can settle when and where to meet.

deeper.text: Wann can be answered with a day or a time. Um wie viel Uhr asks only for the clock time. Choose the question that matches the answer you want. If you want the exact hour, ask Um wie viel Uhr. If you want any time (day or hour), ask Wann.

Each sentence has its own verb in part 2 and its own infinitive at the end. Step 1: no. Step 2: reason. Step 3: smile. The word leider makes it kind. Extra example: Leider muss ich früh aufstehen. = Unfortunately I must get up early.
cards.lead: Not every invitation fits your day. This card shows how to decline in a friendly way and give a reason, so you can say no without sounding unkind.

deeper.text: A refusal sounds friendlier with a reason. Leider muss ich arbeiten is better than only Nein. With a reason the other person understands, and often suggests another day. After muss, a separable verb stays together. Put the reason in the middle and the infinitive at the end.

lessons.title: In the café: order, pay and tip (and the sounds ei, eu, au)
lessons.goal: Order food and drink, understand the price, pay together or separately, and say ei, eu and au.

grammar.point: Order with Ich möchte … or Ich nehme …; nehmen is irregular (du nimmst, er nimmt); pay with Zahlen, bitte! and Zusammen oder getrennt?
grammar.oneLine: Ich nehme den Salat. Zahlen, bitte! Zusammen oder getrennt?

mistake.why: nehmen changes its vowel for du and er/sie: nimmst, nimmt.

terms.meaning: a verb that does not follow the normal pattern: nehmen
extra money you give for good service: Trinkgeld
how letters are said out loud

cards.title: Before we start: in the café
cards.body: You sit in a café. You order, you pay and you decide how much to tip. Today you do all of this in German, and you learn three sound pairs: ei, eu and au.
steps: You already know: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte (chapter 4) and the numbers and Euro
New today: nehmen, Zahlen bitte, Das macht … Euro and Stimmt so
By the end you can: order, pay, and say how you want to tip

examples.en: I would like a coffee, please.

examples.why: New today: a chunk to pay.
New today: Das macht … Euro, the price the waiter says.

cards.more: This lesson is a small play with two actors: you and the waiter. The waiter asks, you answer, and both of you use short, set phrases. Think of them as Lego bricks. You learn each brick as one whole piece and click it together. There is almost no new grammar, just one verb, nehmen, with a small change. The next cards go through ordering, paying and tipping. At the end you practise the sounds ei, eu and au.

cards.title: Order food and drink
cards.body: In a café the waiter (der Kellner) or waitress (die Kellnerin) asks Was möchten Sie? or Was darf es sein? First you ask Die Speisekarte, bitte! Then you order (bestellen) with Ich möchte … or Ich nehme … and bitte. The thing you order is the object: only masculine words change (einen, den).

examples.en: I would like a coffee, please.

cards.more: Think of ordering as a little ping-pong game. The waiter hits: Was möchten Sie? You hit back: Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte. The thing you order is the object, so only the blue masculine box changes: der Kaffee becomes einen Kaffee. The other boxes stay. Step 1: say Ich möchte. Step 2: add what you want. Step 3: say bitte. Extra example: Ich möchte eine Cola, bitte. = I would like a cola, please.
cards.lead: You can now ask for food and drink in a café. This card shows how a waiter asks what you want and how to answer, so you can say you would like a coffee.

deeper.text: Ich will would sound rude in a café, like I want in English. That is why Germans say ich möchte, which is polite. Ich nehme means I will take it and is also very common. Both work, and with bitte they sound even nicer.

cards.title: nehmen: I will take it
cards.body: nehmen (to take) is irregular. The e becomes i for du and er/sie, and the h goes away in du nimmst, er nimmt. ich nehme, du nimmst, er/sie nimmt, wir nehmen. Use it to choose a dish.
cards.more: nehmen is one of the verbs that changes a vowel, like essen and sprechen. For du and er/sie the first e becomes i. And the h is dropped, too: nimmst, nimmt. For ich and wir, nothing changes. Step 1: find the person. Step 2: du or er/sie? Use nimm-. Step 3: add the ending. Extra example: Ben nimmt den Fisch. = Ben takes the fish.
cards.lead: Ordering needs one more verb, the one for choosing a dish. This card gives its forms, so you can say what you will take and what your friend chooses.

deeper.text: nehmen has two changes: e becomes i and the h disappears. Other verbs also change e to i in du and er/sie: essen (to eat) has du isst and er isst. So it is a pattern, not a surprise. Watch for it in du and er/sie, and nowhere else.

cards.title: Paying: Zahlen, bitte!
cards.body: To pay, call the waiter: Zahlen, bitte! or Die Rechnung, bitte! The waiter asks Zusammen oder getrennt? (together or separate?). You answer Zusammen, bitte. or Getrennt, bitte. In Germany it is normal to pay separately.
cards.more: Think of the bill as a cake. Do you eat it together as one, or does everyone pay for their own slice? In Germany it is very common to pay separately. The waiter comes to the table and asks Zusammen oder getrennt? You answer in one word. Step 1: say Zahlen, bitte! Step 2: listen for zusammen or getrennt. Step 3: answer. Extra example: Zusammen, bitte! = Together, please!
cards.lead: After the order comes the bill. This card gives the words to ask for it and to say how you want to pay, so you can finish your visit smoothly.

deeper.text: Zahlen, bitte! is the verb zahlen (to pay) at the start of the sentence: To pay, please. Ich zahle means I pay. Zahlen with a capital Z in the middle of a sentence is the noun die Zahlen (the numbers). Same spelling, different job. Pay attention to the capital.

cards.title: The price: Das macht … Euro
cards.body: The waiter tells you the price: Das macht 14 Euro 80. You know the numbers and Euro from chapter 4. Say the Euro first and then the Cent: vierzehn Euro achtzig. macht here means it comes to.
cards.more: You already know prices from the shop. Here the waiter says Das macht, which is like in English That makes. Then the amount. Step 1: hear Das macht. Step 2: listen for the Euro number. Step 3: listen for the Cent number, if there is one. Step 4: pay. Extra example: Das macht 9 Euro 50. = That comes to 9 euros 50.
cards.lead: The waiter will tell you a price, often with cents. This card shows how to say euros and cents out loud, so you can understand the total.

deeper.text: Spoken prices drop the word Cent: 14,80 € is vierzehn Euro achtzig. In writing, German uses a comma where English uses a point: 14,80, and a dot where English has a comma: 1.000. It is the opposite way round, so look carefully at prices.

cards.title: Tipping: Trinkgeld and Stimmt so
cards.body: In Germany you tip about 5 to 10 per cent. You do not leave money on the table. You say the total you want to pay: Zwanzig Euro, stimmt so. Stimmt so means keep the change. It is the tip.
cards.more: A tip is a little thank you. In a restaurant the waiter does not put the tip in a box. You round up the price. The bill is 18 Euro. You say Zwanzig Euro, stimmt so, and give 20 Euro. The waiter keeps the 2 Euro extra. Step 1: hear the price. Step 2: round up a little. Step 3: say stimmt so. Extra example: Das macht 9 Euro 50. Zehn Euro, stimmt so! = That is 9.50. Ten euros, keep the change!
cards.lead: Paying is nearly done, and in Germany you usually add a little extra. This card shows how to say the amount you want to pay and keep the change, so you can leave a tip.

deeper.text: stimmt comes from stimmen, which means to be correct. Das stimmt! is a very common reply: That is right. So Stimmt so means it is correct like that: no change. This one verb is useful in many chats. You can also say Das stimmt nicht, which means That is not right.

cards.title: The sounds ei, eu and au
cards.body: Three letter pairs, three sounds. ei sounds like English eye: Eis, zwei. eu sounds like oy: Euro, neu. au sounds like ow in cow: Auto, auf. Careful: ie is different. ie says ee, like in Bier.
cards.more: The two letters make one sound, like a little team. ei is not ee. It sounds like the English word eye. Try it: zwei, Eis, Freitag. eu is not you. It sounds like oy in boy: Euro, neu, heute. au sounds like ow in cow: Auto, auf, Haus. Step 1: spot the pair. Step 2: say the team sound. Step 3: say the word. Extra example: Das Haus ist neu. = The house is new.
cards.lead: Sounds come last. Three letter pairs sound different from English, so you can say Eis and Auto clearly.

deeper.text: Mixing up ei and ie is a very common spelling mistake, because the sounds swap. Here is a trick: the second letter names the sound. ei says i, like the English eye. ie says e, like ee. So Wein (wine) and Wien (Vienna) sound different.

lessons.title: Accusative pronouns: mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch
lessons.goal: Use pronouns as objects and swap a noun for the right pronoun.

grammar.point: A pronoun as an object changes: ich → mich, du → dich, er → ihn, wir → uns, ihr → euch; sie, es and Sie stay the same
grammar.oneLine: Ich rufe dich an. Der Kuchen ist lecker. Ich esse ihn.

mistake.why: When du is the object, it becomes dich.

terms.meaning: who does the action: Mira in Mira ruft an
who or what receives the action
the object form: den, ihn, mich, dich

cards.title: Before we start: me, you, him and her as objects
cards.body: Mira calls me. I call you. Anna sees us. People can be the object of a sentence, and so can things. Today you learn the object forms of the little words ich, du and er.
steps: You already know: der becomes den as the object, nothing else changes (chapter 4)
New today: the pronouns as objects, mich, dich, ihn, uns, euch
By the end you can: say Ich rufe dich an and Ich esse ihn

examples.de: Der Kuchen ist lecker. Ich esse den Kuchen.
examples.en: The cake is tasty. I eat the cake.

examples.de: Der Kuchen ist lecker. Ich esse ihn.
examples.en: The cake is tasty. I eat it.
examples.why: New today: er becomes ihn, just like der becomes den.
New today: ich becomes mich as the object.

cards.more: You learned that only masculine words change when they are the object, der to den. The little pronoun words follow the very same idea. Er becomes ihn, because the masculine word changes. Sie and es stay the same. The two pronouns for me and you change too: mich and dich. Think of it as a costume change for when someone receives the action. You will see all of them in a table and then practise where each one goes in the sentence.

cards.title: Pronouns as objects: mich and dich
cards.body: You know ich, du, er … They are the subject: who does it. A pronoun can also be the object: the person who receives the action. Then ich becomes mich and du becomes dich. This is the accusative, like den for der.
cards.more: Look at who does and who gets. In Mira ruft mich an, Mira does the calling (subject). I get called (object). In English too: I becomes me. German does the same: ich becomes mich. And du becomes dich. Step 1: who does it? Subject. Step 2: who gets it? Object. Step 3: change the pronoun. Extra example: Anna sieht mich. = Anna sees me.
cards.lead: You can say who does an action. Now you learn the small words for the person who receives it, like me and you, so you can say someone calls you.

deeper.text: English also changes its pronouns when they are the object: I see him, not I see he. So German is not so strange. English: I becomes me. German: ich becomes mich. The change is the same idea, only German has more of them. Learn the pairs.

cards.title: er becomes ihn: the same as der → den
cards.body: A pronoun can stand for a thing. In chapter 4 only masculine changed: der → den. The pronoun does the same: er becomes ihn. sie stays sie. es stays es. So: Der Kuchen ist lecker. Ich esse ihn.

examples.de: Der Kuchen ist lecker. Ich esse ihn.
examples.en: The cake is tasty. I eat it.

examples.de: Die Torte ist lecker. Ich esse sie.
examples.en: The cake is tasty. I eat it.

examples.de: Das Eis ist lecker. Ich esse es.
examples.en: The ice cream is tasty. I eat it.

cards.more: Remember the three boxes: blue der, red die, green das. Only the blue box changes when it is the object: der becomes den. The pronoun for the blue box is er, and it changes in the same way: er becomes ihn. The red sie and the green es stay the same. Step 1: find the gender of the noun. Step 2: er, sie or es. Step 3: only er changes: ihn. Extra example: Der Saft ist kalt. Ich trinke ihn. = The juice is cold. I drink it.
cards.lead: Pronouns can also stand in for things. This card shows the object form for a masculine, feminine and neuter thing, so you can say you eat it, whatever its gender.

deeper.text: ihn can mean him (a man) or it (a masculine thing). The pronoun depends on the grammatical gender, not on the meaning. So der Kuchen is er, and as an object ihn. That is the same as English he and him, but for things too. Choose the pronoun by the noun.

cards.title: uns, euch, sie and Sie
cards.body: More changes: wir becomes uns. ihr becomes euch. sie (they) stays sie. Sie (polite you) stays Sie. A person can also be sie (she). So Ich sehe sie can mean I see her or I see them.

examples.de: Ich rufe Sie an, Frau Weber.

cards.more: Only some pronouns change. The rest stay the same. wir becomes uns. ihr becomes euch. And these do not change at all: sie (she), sie (they), es and Sie (polite). So how do you tell sie (she) from sie (they)? As a subject the verb ending tells you: sie sieht is she, sie sehen is they. As an object only the story tells you. Step 1: find the pronoun. Step 2: look it up in the table. Step 3: swap. Extra example: Ben sieht uns. = Ben sees us.
cards.lead: You have pronouns for one person and for things. This card covers the plural ones for us and you all, and the polite you, so you can greet a group or a teacher.

deeper.text: Capital letters help with the polite form. Ich rufe Sie an, Frau Weber means you, but Ich rufe sie an means her or them. In speech there is no capital to hear, so the situation decides: if Frau Weber stands in front of you, Sie means her. In writing the polite Sie always keeps its capital S, even in the middle of a sentence.

cards.title: The full table: nominative and accusative
cards.body: Here are all the pronouns together. Five change: mich, dich, ihn, uns, euch. Four stay the same: sie (she), es, sie (they), Sie. Learn the five that change. Use the accusative when the pronoun is the object.
cards.more: Look at the table like a mirror. On the left you see who does. On the right you see who gets. Only five words on the right look different from the left: mich, dich, ihn, uns, euch. Say them in a row: mich, dich, ihn, uns, euch. Say it ten times. Step 1: say the five. Step 2: check the rest: sie, es, sie, Sie stay. Extra example: Er sieht mich. = He sees me.
cards.lead: Here is the whole set of pronouns in one place. This card puts the subject and the object forms side by side, so you can check any form at a glance.

deeper.text: Learn the five that change as pairs: ich–mich, du–dich, er–ihn, wir–uns, ihr–euch. Say them aloud and listen to the rhyme: ich–mich rhymes, and du–dich both start with d. The pairs make a little chant. After a few times you will say them without thinking.

cards.title: Where does the pronoun go?
cards.body: The pronoun sits right behind the verb and the subject. With a separable verb the prefix still goes last. With a modal the infinitive goes last. Heute rufe ich dich an. Kannst du mich anrufen?

examples.de: Ich möchte dich am Samstag sehen.
examples.en: I would like to see you on Saturday.

examples.why: einladen: the pronoun comes before the prefix.

examples.de: Leon holt uns um 18 Uhr ab.
examples.en: Leon picks us up at 6 pm.

cards.more: The pronoun is short, so it moves close to the front, right behind the verb and the subject. The prefix and the infinitive stay at the very end. Step 1: part 1. Step 2: the verb. Step 3: the subject if it is not in part 1. Step 4: the pronoun. Step 5: other words. Step 6: the prefix or the infinitive at the end. Extra example: Ich rufe dich morgen an. = I call you tomorrow.
cards.lead: Pronouns have a fixed place in the sentence. This card shows where they sit with a split verb and with a modal, so you can put your words in the right order.

deeper.text: Pronouns are short, so they come early. The pronoun comes before time words: Ich rufe dich heute an. A noun comes later: Ich rufe heute Mira an. So short words go left and long things go right. This is the same pattern as with the separable verbs, which end the sentence.

cards.title: Who do you mean? wen?
cards.body: Ask about a person who is the object with Wen? It means whom. Wen rufst du an? Ich rufe Mira an. Or with a pronoun: Ich rufe sie an. Wen triffst du? Kennst du ihn? (kennen = to know a person.)

examples.en: Whom do you meet on Saturday?

cards.more: You know wer? = who. When the answer is the object, who becomes wen: whom. It is the same idea as den and ihn: the question word changes when it is the object. Step 1: ask Wen …? Step 2: the verb comes in part 2. Step 3: answer with a name or a pronoun. Extra example: Wen siehst du? Ich sehe ihn. = Whom do you see? I see him.
cards.lead: Your question words now need to ask about a person. This card gives the question for whom, so you can ask who someone is calling or meeting.

deeper.text: wer asks about the subject: who does it. wen asks about the object: who gets it. wen is the accusative of wer. English has the same pair, who and whom, but most people no longer use whom. German still uses wen every day. So Wen? is a very common question.

lessons.title: für + accusative: für mich, für dich, für den Vater
lessons.goal: Say who something is for and ask Für wen?

grammar.point: für is always followed by the accusative: für mich, für dich, für ihn; für den Vater (only masculine changes)

mistake.why: After für use the object form: dich, not du.

terms.meaning: a little word that links: für, in, mit
the object form: mich, dich, ihn, den
wen: the question word for a person who is the object

cards.title: Before we start: for someone
cards.body: This present is for you. This cake is for my father. Whom is it for? Today you learn one small word, für, and the rule that comes with it: after für you use the object form.
steps: You already know: der → den and ich → mich as objects
New today: für, which always takes the object form
By the end you can: say Das Geschenk ist für dich and ask Für wen?

examples.de: Ich kaufe ein Geschenk für Mira.
examples.en: I buy a present for Mira.
examples.why: New today: für says who it is for.
New today: after für, ich becomes mich.

cards.more: Some little words are like bouncers: when they stand in front of a person, that person must wear the object costume. Für is one of those. It has no exceptions, which is great news. So after für, ich is always mich, du is always dich, and der Vater is always den Vater. You already know the costumes from the last lessons. In the next cards you practise them with für, step by step.

cards.title: für = for, and für takes the accusative
cards.body: für means for. After für you always use the accusative, the object form. So pronouns change: für mich, für dich, für ihn. This is a little rule with no exceptions: für + accusative.
cards.more: Some little words always make the next word wear the object form. für is one of them. Whenever you see für, switch to the accusative. Step 1: write für. Step 2: look at the person. Step 3: use the object form of the pronoun: mich, dich, ihn. It is the same table as in the last lesson. Extra example: Das Essen ist für uns. = The food is for us.
cards.lead: You know the object forms now. This card adds one small word, für, that comes with a set of forms, so you can say who a gift is for.

deeper.text: für always takes the accusative, so it is a good chance to practise. Ich becomes mich: für mich. Do not say für ich. English works the same: for me, not for I. So you already feel that it is right. This is one of the easiest rules in German.

cards.title: für + a noun: only masculine changes
cards.body: After für the noun has the accusative form, too. Only masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen. die, das and eine, ein stay. Here are family words: der Vater (father) and die Mutter (mother).

cards.more: Do you remember the blue box from chapter 4? Only the blue masculine box changes in the accusative: der becomes den, ein becomes einen. This works after für, too. The red and the green box stay the same. Step 1: find the gender. Step 2: masculine? den or einen. Step 3: other? keep it. Extra example: Der Tee ist für einen Freund. = The tea is for a friend.
cards.lead: After für a noun also takes its object form. This card shows the change for masculine nouns after für, so you can say a cake is for the father.

deeper.text: Remember the pattern from chapter 4: only der and ein change. For feminine and neuter words nothing happens. In the plural there is no change either: für die Eltern. Eltern is always plural, so it is always die. So the family words give you all four forms.

example.de: Das Buch ist für den Bruder.
example.en: The book is for the brother.

cards.title: A present for someone, and thank you for it
cards.body: Put the für part after the object: Ich kaufe ein Geschenk für Mira. You can also thank someone with Danke für …: Danke für die Einladung! Danke für das Geschenk! Both use the accusative.

cards.more: A sentence can have two little groups after the verb. The thing you buy (object). And who it is for (für + accusative). Think of two boxes: What? and For whom? Step 1: Ich kaufe (the verb). Step 2: What? ein Geschenk. Step 3: For whom? für Mira. Names never change. Danke für … is a chunk you can use at once. Extra example: Danke für das Geschenk! = Thanks for the present!
cards.lead: You can now say who something is for. This card shows where the für part goes in a sentence, and how to thank someone with it, so you can say thanks for an invitation.

deeper.text: Danke für is a pattern worth owning: Danke für + thing. English says thank you for the … and works the same way. After für use the accusative, so a masculine word changes: Danke für den Kaffee! Feminine and neuter stay: die Einladung, das Geschenk.

cards.title: Ask: Für wen?
cards.body: To ask who something is for, say Für wen? You know wen (whom) from the last lesson. Für wen ist das? Für wen kaufst du ein Geschenk? Answer: Für Anna. or Für ihn.

examples.de: Für wen kaufst du ein Geschenk?
examples.en: Who are you buying a present for?

rows: Für wen kaufst du ein Geschenk?

cards.more: Start the question with für. Then the question word wen. They go together: für wen. That is the first part of the sentence. Then comes the verb in part 2, as always. Step 1: für wen. Step 2: the verb. Step 3: the rest. Step 4: answer with für + name or für + pronoun. Extra example: Für wen ist die Blume? Für die Mutter. = Who is the flower for? For the mother.
cards.lead: The question for whom needs one more word. This card shows how to ask who something is for and how to answer, so you can talk about a gift with a friend.

deeper.text: Für wen? is two words, and the preposition comes first. English can split them: Who is it for? German always keeps für and wen together at the start. So the question is Für wen? and never Wen für? Notice that wen has the accusative form after für.

cards.title: Time and a table for two
cards.body: für is also used for other things. Hast du Zeit für mich? asks if you have time for me. In a restaurant: Einen Tisch für zwei, bitte. A table for two, please. The number needs no ending.

examples.en: Do you have time for me?

cards.more: Think of für as a little arrow pointing at the person or number it is for. Time for me. A table for two. After für the pronoun is always the accusative, and a number just stays the number. Step 1: say what: Zeit or einen Tisch. Step 2: für. Step 3: who or how many. Extra example: Ich habe keine Zeit für dich. = I have no time for you.
cards.lead: Für is not only for gifts. This card shows two more everyday uses, one about time and one about a table, so you can ask for someone's time or book a table.

deeper.text: für also tells how many people a table is for: Einen Tisch für zwei is a table for two. In a restaurant you can ask politely with Sie: Haben Sie einen Tisch für zwei? einen is used because Tisch is masculine and it is the thing you want. The number after für needs no ending, so für drei, für vier and für zehn all work.

cards.more: Use the same three questions every time. Question 1: what comes after für? Question 2: pronoun or noun? Question 3: a pronoun uses the table; a noun uses den or einen only if it is masculine. Spot it, fix it, done. Step 1: für. Step 2: ask. Step 3: answer. Extra example: Das Geschenk ist für sie. = The present is for her.
cards.lead: This last card is a method for spotting für in any sentence. Check three things and you will know which form to use, so you can read and write it without guessing.

lessons.title: war and hatte: talking about yesterday and last weekend
lessons.goal: Use war and hatte in all six forms to describe an event that has happened.

grammar.point: The simple past of sein is war, of haben is hatte; ich and er/sie/es have no ending; the verb stays in part 2
grammar.oneLine: Gestern war ich müde. Wir hatten viel Zeit.

mistake.why: For yesterday use the past form war, not bin.

terms.meaning: what has already happened: yesterday, last week
the past of sein: was, were
the past of haben: had

cards.title: Before we start: yesterday
cards.body: How was the party? Were you tired yesterday? To talk about the past you do not need a lot yet. Two small verbs are enough: war and hatte, the past of sein and haben.
steps: You already know: sein and haben in all six forms (chapter 2)
New today: war and hatte, the past forms
By the end you can: say Gestern war ich müde and ask Wo warst du gestern?

examples.why: New today: war is the past of bin.
New today: hatte is the past of habe.

cards.more: Think of sein and haben as two old friends who each own a second outfit for yesterday. Bin turns into war, habe turns into hatte. The sentence itself works the same way: the verb is in chair 2 in a statement and first in a yes/no question. So you only learn two short outfits, each with six forms. In the next cards you learn the forms, time words like gestern, and how to describe an event that was great or loud.

cards.title: The past of sein and haben: war and hatte
cards.body: To talk about yesterday or last weekend, use war (was) for sein and hatte (had) for haben. These are short past forms. They are the easiest way to talk about the past in German. Now: ich bin müde. Yesterday: ich war müde.

examples.de: Am Samstag war ich in Hamburg.
examples.en: On Saturday I was in Hamburg.

cards.more: Imagine a time machine. In the present you say ich bin and ich habe. Step in the machine and the words change: ich war, ich hatte. The sentence order stays the same. Step 1: say the time word: gestern. Step 2: the past verb in part 2: war or hatte. Step 3: the rest. Extra example: Gestern hatte ich Zeit. = Yesterday I had time.
cards.lead: Your intro asked how the party was. This card gives the past forms of the two most common verbs, so you can say how you were or what you had yesterday.

deeper.text: Native speakers use war and hatte all the time in everyday speech. For most other verbs people use a different past, which you learn later. So war and hatte are your shortcut for describing how things were. They look like English too: war is was, and both start with w.

cards.title: war: all forms
cards.body: Learn all six forms of war. ich war, du warst, er/sie/es war, wir waren, ihr wart, sie/Sie waren. ich and er/sie/es have no ending: both are war. The rest add -st, -en, -t, -en.

examples.de: Wir waren am Samstag in Hamburg.
examples.en: We were in Hamburg on Saturday.
You (all) were in the café yesterday.

cards.more: war is irregular, like sein, so learn the list by heart. Look at the pattern: ich and er/sie/es are the same word, war. The others look a lot like the normal endings: du warst, wir waren, ihr wart, sie waren. Say the list out loud: war, warst, war, waren, wart, waren. Step 1: find the person. Step 2: pick the form. Extra example: Sie waren im Kino. = They were at the cinema.
cards.lead: You have one past form now. This card gives all six forms of war, so you can say who was tired, who was where and who was at a party.

deeper.text: The w in German sounds like English v, so war sounds like vahr. English helps: ich war is I was, and wir waren is we were. The forms ich war and er war are the same, as in English. The polite form uses the same verb as sie: Sie waren.

cards.title: hatte: all forms
cards.body: Learn all six forms of hatte. ich hatte, du hattest, er/sie/es hatte, wir hatten, ihr hattet, sie/Sie hatten. It is like war: ich and er/sie/es have no ending. The rest add -st, -n, -t, -n to hatte.

examples.en: Anna had her birthday on Saturday.
We had a lot of time.

cards.more: hatte works like war. The base is hatte. Then you add: ich hatte, du hattest, er hatte, wir hatten, ihr hattet, sie hatten. Be careful: du hattest has an extra -st, and wir hatten has -n. Step 1: find the person. Step 2: pick the form from the table. Step 3: put it in part 2. Extra example: Ihr hattet Zeit. = You (all) had time.
cards.lead: The second past form works in the same way. This card gives all six forms of hatte, so you can say what each person had on a past day.

deeper.text: hatte is built from the stem hatt- plus the usual past endings: -e, -est, -e, -en, -et, -en. So ich hatte and er hatte look the same. Mind the double t: hat (now) has one t, hatte (past) has two. Germans use hatte a lot: Ich hatte Hunger says you were hungry, and Ich hatte einen schönen Tag says you had a nice day.

cards.title: Word order and questions with war and hatte
cards.body: The word order does not change. The verb is part 2 in statements and W-questions, and part 1 in yes/no questions. Wo warst du gestern? Wie war das Fest? Hattest du Zeit?

examples.en: Did you have time on Saturday?

cards.more: You already know this word order from chapters 1 and 2. W-question: question word first, verb second. Yes/no question: verb first. Only the verb is new: war and hatte. Step 1: choose the question type. Step 2: put in war, warst, hatte or hattest. Step 3: add the rest. Extra example: Wie war das Konzert? Super! = How was the concert? Great!
cards.lead: Past sentences keep the same word order you know. This card shows how to ask questions about yesterday, so you can ask where someone was or if they had time.

deeper.text: English also uses the same word order. Where were you? has the question word first, then the verb, then the subject. Were you at home? has the verb first. German does exactly the same. So war and hatte give you the same shapes as in the present. Only the verb is new.

cards.title: When? gestern, letzte Woche, letztes Wochenende
cards.body: Time words tell you it is past. gestern (yesterday). Learn these as chunks: letzte Woche (last week), letztes Wochenende (last weekend), letzten Samstag (last Saturday). You will see why the endings look like this later.

examples.de: Letzte Woche war ich in Wien.
examples.en: Last week I was in Vienna.

examples.de: Letzten Samstag war ich im Kino.
examples.en: Last Saturday I was at the cinema.
Last week I had a holiday.

cards.more: Each of these is one little block, like a Lego brick. letzte Woche. letztes Wochenende. letzten Samstag. You do not need to know why they look different. Just pick the block and put it in part 1. The verb is then in part 2 and the subject follows it. Step 1: pick the time block. Step 2: war or hatte. Step 3: the subject. Step 4: the rest. Extra example: Gestern war ich in Hamburg. = Yesterday I was in Hamburg.
cards.lead: Your past sentences need time words. This card gives phrases for yesterday, last week and last weekend, so you can say when something happened.

deeper.text: The ending of letzte tells the gender of the word after it: die Woche → letzte Woche, das Wochenende → letztes Wochenende, der Samstag → letzten Samstag. You do not need the rule now. Just learn the three chunks and put them at the start of a story.

example.de: Letzten Sonntag war ich zu Hause.
example.en: Last Sunday I was at home.

cards.title: Describe an event: war for things
cards.body: war works for things and events, too: das Konzert war super, es war laut. In the present you say ist. In the past you say war. Use sein + a describing word: no ending. Add nicht or sehr before it.

examples.de: Der Film war lustig, nicht langweilig.
examples.en: The film was fun, not boring.

cards.more: Tell a short story. Say where you were: war ich in Hamburg. Say what you had: hatten wir Zeit. Say how it was: das Konzert war super. These three small sentences tell an event. After war there is no ending on the describing word, just like after ist. Step 1: where. Step 2: what you had. Step 3: how it was. Extra example: Das Fest war laut, aber schön. = The party was loud, but lovely.
cards.lead: The past form works for things and events too, not only for people. This card shows how to describe how something was, so you can say a concert was great.

deeper.text: After war and ist, a describing word stands alone with no ending, like in English: it was good. So Das Essen war lecker, not leckere. Words that describe an event are often warm: toll (great) is a favourite after a party. Adding sehr (very) makes it stronger.
